business.contact_alt_html: Prefer chat? Message us on Telegram.
business.contact_text: Tell us what you are building. An engineer answers, not a sales script.
business.hero_lede: Commercial support, custom development, and OEM licensing from the core team.
business.hero_title: Build your product on OpenIPC — with the people who build OpenIPC.
business.how1: You write to us with the product and the problem.
business.how2: A scoping call with an engineer.
business.how4: Ongoing support or development, sized to your needs.
business.licensing_html: The core of the platform is MIT-licensed — commercial use is welcome. The Majestic streamer is distributed in binary form under the Prosperity license; commercial terms are available. The use of OpenIPC and its components for military purposes is not permitted.
business.offer1_text: Priority fixes, guaranteed response times, and long-term maintenance of the platforms your product depends on.
business.offer2_text: SoC bring-up, sensor tuning, NPU features, custom video links, white-label firmware — built to your specification by the people who know the stack best.
business.offer3_text: Commercial licensing for Majestic, branded builds, and integration help for manufacturers shipping OpenIPC-based products.
business.service_digital_twins_text: Your unmodified firmware in the loop as a model: test overnight, gate in CI.
business.service_edge_ai_text: Neural inference on the camera chip, at the speed the silicon was sold for.
business.service_isp_sensors_text: The frame rate the datasheet promised: sensor ports and pipeline tuning on four silicon vendors.
business.service_reverse_engineering_text: Blobs to source, protocols to specifications, models to layouts, every claim verified on hardware.
business.service_teleoperation_text: Video and control for remote operation at the latency the task needs.
business.service_turnkey_hardware_text: Board and firmware from one team, so the product is balanced from the schematic on.
business.service_video_encoding_text: The same encoder, fewer bits: hardware and codec tuning measured on your content.
business.title: For Business
business.why1_text: Vendor SDKs give you a kernel and a demo. OpenIPC gives you a shipping firmware with streaming, web interface, and updates — you start from 90%, not from zero.
business.why2_text: Our mainline-kernel work keeps platforms maintained after vendors abandon them. Your product's lifespan is not capped by a vendor's roadmap.
business.why3_text: Devices work without our servers — or anyone's. Your cost structure stays yours.
business.why4_text: The core is open. Whatever happens to any company, including ours, your product keeps building.

community.contrib2_text: Fork the code, make your improvement, send a pull request. Small fixes are welcome — that is how most of us started.
community.contrib3_text: Run work-in-progress builds on your hardware and tell us what breaks. First adopters are what moves a platform from WIP to DONE.

community.help3: When you ask, include the SoC, the sensor, what you tried, and a boot log if you have one. Good questions get fast answers.

digital_twins.bring1_text: Your production image boots in the model — the same bytes you ship. No test build, no stubbed drivers, nothing to argue about later.
digital_twins.bring2_text: Byte-identical results across processes, gated in CI, so a fault found at three in the morning reproduces at nine. A single microsecond of input difference is visible as a different run.
digital_twins.bring3_text: Vision engine pixel for pixel, radio bit for bit, controller trace for trace. The twin's agreement with the hardware is itself a test that runs on every push.
digital_twins.bring4_text: Thousands of flights, links or boots a night on one machine, with fault injection, fading, collisions and sensor noise that a bench cannot schedule.
digital_twins.bring4_title: Scale that finds the rare fault
digital_twins.brings_intro: Four things, each one measured on the hardware.
digital_twins.cta_note_html: Commercial support, OEM licensing and the other services are on the business page.
digital_twins.cta_text: One mail with four lines: the system, the test you cannot run today, what you can share, and where the tests should run. An engineer answers with a plan, not a sales script.
digital_twins.cta_title: Send the firmware and the test you cannot run. In fifteen days it will run.
digital_twins.eyebrow: Whitepaper · Digital twins · Safety-critical systems tested without the hardware
digital_twins.hero_cta_send: Send us the test you cannot run
digital_twins.hero_lede: A device you cannot crash, a radio you cannot jam, a flight you cannot afford to repeat: put the hardware in the loop as a model instead. We build twins that boot your unmodified firmware, reproduce your radio bit for bit and run your controller a thousand times before breakfast, gated in CI on every push.
digital_twins.hero_title: Take the hardware out of the loop — and test overnight what took a season.
digital_twins.meta_description: Digital-twin environments for safety-critical systems: unmodified firmware booting in emulation, radios reproduced bit for bit on software radio, controllers run thousands of times a night, validated against silicon and gated in CI.
digital_twins.platforms_text: Twins are delivered as CI jobs with the validation suite that proves them, so the agreement between the model and the hardware is a number your pipeline checks, not a claim in a report.
digital_twins.pull_quote: The device under test leaves the loop. The proof stays.
digital_twins.res1_text: 45 camera-SoC machines boot unmodified firmware on the desktop, with the vision engine emulated and validated pixel for pixel against the chip. Every push to the driver runs against the twin before it touches a board, so bring-up bugs are found in CI, not on the bench.
digital_twins.res2_text: Wi-Fi up to the current generation is transmitted and received on software radio, 35 configurations bit-exact, and used to validate our own driver on air. On a physical model of the link, a learned controller beat the measured-evidence controller under fading on both counts — less energy and more delivery — with the model kept tick for tick in step with what ships.
digital_twins.res3_text: A flight-controller simulator runs the pilot's real firmware with byte-identical determinism, virtual motor controllers, collision physics and a training environment. The same method reaches robots: on our desktop AI system a humanoid trains on rough terrain at 63,000 simulation steps a second, with video of every run rendered without a screen.
digital_twins.scar_p1: With the hardware in the loop, every test is bounded by how many units you have, how many people can hold them, and how many crashes the budget allows. The rare fault — the one certification asks about — shows up once a quarter and never on the bench.
digital_twins.scar_p2: A model that is nearly right is a liability: it passes tests the hardware fails. A twin earns trust only when it is checked against silicon — frame against frame, packet against packet, run against run — and when that check runs on every commit, not once at the start.
digital_twins.scar_title: Your test plan is bounded by how many units you can afford to break
digital_twins.stat1_l: camera-SoC machines booting unmodified production firmware in emulation, the vision engine validated pixel for pixel against silicon
digital_twins.stat2_l: Wi-Fi configurations transmitted and received bit-exact on software radio, up to Wi-Fi 6
digital_twins.stat3_l: simulation steps a second training a humanoid on rough terrain, on one desktop system
digital_twins.stats_source: The first two run in our CI on every push; the third was measured on our own desktop AI system.
digital_twins.step1_text: Fixed price, fifteen working days. You send the firmware image or controller, the hardware — a unit or its documentation — and the test you cannot run today. You get your firmware booting in a first model, or your controller running in the simulator, the validation plan against silicon, and a fixed quote for the full twin.
digital_twins.step2_text: Build the twin to the fidelity the test needs, validate it against your hardware, and install it in your CI with the agreement check as a gate.
digital_twins.step3_text: The twin, its validation suite and the CI jobs are yours; your team extends it as the product changes, and the gate keeps telling the truth.
digital_twins.title: Digital twins

donate.accounting: We're committed to open and transparent accounting, and are grateful for any support you can provide to our efforts to advance OpenIPC and our mission toward a sustainable future.
donate.business_band_html: If your company depends on OpenIPC, the sustainable way to support it is a commercial relationship. See what we offer.
donate.hero_lede: OpenIPC is free to use and expensive to make. Donations buy cameras for new platforms, pay maintainers, and keep the lights on.
donate.oc_text_html: Recurring or one-time, with open and transparent accounting. Recurring backers are permanently listed in the Sponsors section on our GitHub page.
donate.thanks: Thank you. It means more than you think.
donate.title: Donate
donate.where_text: Core team members spend their own money on cameras and SDK access to expand hardware support. Funds ease that burden, compensate part-time maintainers, and cover trade shows and vendor meetings where hardware partnerships actually happen.

ecosystem.contribute_cta_html: Pick a project and make it better. Start here.
ecosystem.hero_lede: OpenIPC is an ecosystem of more than a hundred open repositories: the firmware itself, the video pipeline, the tools around it, and the research that keeps old silicon alive.
ecosystem.proj_aviateur: Cross-platform receiver: watch the link on Windows, Linux, or macOS.
ecosystem.proj_coupler: The smooth migration path from vendor firmware to OpenIPC and back. No soldering, no special skills.
ecosystem.proj_devourer: The link itself: a userspace driver for Realtek Wi-Fi adapters, setting rate, power, and channel packet by packet.
ecosystem.proj_divinus: An open-source streamer for a growing set of platforms.
ecosystem.proj_firmware: Universal, Buildroot-based firmware for IP cameras — replaces abandoned vendor systems on dozens of SoC families.
ecosystem.proj_ipctool: Identifies the SoC, sensor, and flash chip of nearly any camera — and backs up the stock firmware before you change anything.
ecosystem.proj_majestic: The streamer at the heart of the firmware: RTSP, ONVIF, WebRTC, HLS, audio, night modes. Distributed as a binary under the Prosperity license; commercial terms available.
ecosystem.proj_microbe: The web interface of the firmware.
ecosystem.proj_onvif_tt: An ONVIF conformance test tool: verify what a camera actually implements. Free.
ecosystem.proj_openhisilicon: Keeps the HiSilicon vendor SDK alive on mainline kernels — CVE fixes and modern features after the vendor walks away.
ecosystem.proj_openxiongmai: The same idea for Xiongmai SoCs: an open SDK replacement.
ecosystem.proj_pixelpilot: The RX side: turns a Rockchip board into a dedicated ground station with display output.
ecosystem.proj_qemu: A full HiSilicon IP camera emulator on QEMU — develop and test firmware without hardware on your desk.
ecosystem.proj_rnd_player: A player built for media engineers: inspect streams the way a developer needs to.
ecosystem.proj_smolrtsp: An embeddable RTSP 1.0 server library for cameras and other constrained devices. TCP and UDP, any payload format.
ecosystem.proj_waybeam: The TX side of the link: a flexible video encoder for FPV drones and URLLC devices.
ecosystem.proj_yamlcli: A small console tool for editing YAML configs from scripts.
ecosystem.section_community_text_html: User-made hardware, mounts, and accessories — like the 3D-printable models tagged openipc on Printables.
ecosystem.section_core_text: The operating system, the streamer, and the tools that get you from stock firmware to OpenIPC.
ecosystem.section_longevity_text: Vendor SDKs assume vendor kernels: ancient, unpatched, abandoned. We port them to mainline — CVE fixes and modern kernel features long after end-of-life.
ecosystem.section_lowlat_text_html: The open video link for drones, robots, and teleoperation. Read the overview.
ecosystem.section_tools_text: Free tools for camera and media engineers — useful even if you never flash our firmware.
ecosystem.stage_legend_html: Every project carries an honest status badge — the same vocabulary we use for firmware platforms. How stages work.
ecosystem.title: Ecosystem

edge_ai.bring_driver_text: Cleanroom kernel drivers for HiSilicon's vision and neural engines, built from disassembly and kernel tracing, byte-identical to the vendor's own — and more robust where the vendor's test hangs. Vendor silence is not a blocker.
edge_ai.bring_driver_title: Where there is no driver, we write one
edge_ai.bring_fit_text: Models reshaped so the whole network runs on the accelerator instead of half of it, and retrained on the camera's own picture: its angle, its image pipeline, its native scale. A model moved to a new camera without that step loses ten to twenty points of accuracy.
edge_ai.bring_fit_title: Fit the model to the chip and the camera
edge_ai.bring_map_text: We have mapped four NPU families by running models on them, not by reading the vendor's PDF: what runs on the accelerator, what silently falls back, and what to change before you spend a sprint finding out.
edge_ai.bring_map_title: We know what your NPU cannot run
edge_ai.bring_proven_text: The vision engine runs in CI under our own QEMU, validated pixel for pixel against the silicon. Every change is tested overnight on emulated hardware, so the bench is not the bottleneck and your board is not on our desk.
edge_ai.bring_proven_title: Proven before it touches a board
edge_ai.brings_intro: Four things, each one measured on silicon.
edge_ai.cta_note_html: Camera firmware, sensor tuning and custom video links are on the business page.
edge_ai.cta_text: One mail with four lines: the model and its format, the target SoC and SDK version, a link to frames from the camera, and the fps and accuracy you need. An engineer answers with a plan, not a sales script.
edge_ai.cta_title: Send the model and the SoC. Get a verdict in a week.
edge_ai.eyebrow: Whitepaper · Edge AI · Inference on the camera chip
edge_ai.hero_art_alt: A night car park where a neural network converges onto two cars whose licence plates are outlined
edge_ai.hero_cta_send: Send us your model and your SoC
edge_ai.hero_lede: AI inference on camera-SoC NPUs and vision engines, at the speed the silicon was sold for, on hardware nobody hands you the tools for. From the team behind OpenIPC.
edge_ai.hero_title: You have the model and the chip. We make them run together.
edge_ai.meta_description: AI inference on camera-SoC NPUs and vision engines: what four NPU families can run, drivers where the vendor has none, models fitted to the chip and the camera, tested in CI without a board.
edge_ai.platforms_text: We ship firmware on all of them and work under NDA with most camera-SoC vendors, including toolchains that are not distributed outside their home market. If your chip is not on the list, ask: the answer is a yes or a no within 48 hours.
edge_ai.pull_quote: The wall is the toolchain, not your model.
edge_ai.res_cpu_text: On cameras with no accelerator at all, our own integer engine made a neural classifier run five times faster on the camera's single core, with the same answers as the reference. Detection wakes only when the hardware motion engine sees something move, so a quiet scene costs nothing.
edge_ai.res_faces_text: Detection and recognition in eight milliseconds, entirely on the accelerator, from a model small enough to live beside the video pipeline — and as accurate on the standard benchmark as models many times its size.
edge_ai.res_plates_text: Plates found and read at more than eighty frames a second on a camera chip's accelerator, with nothing given up to make the model fit. Trained on the camera's own picture, so it reads what the lens actually sees, at night, in a car park, at the angle the camera hangs.
edge_ai.scar_p1: A camera SoC's NPU is not a GPU. It runs its own short list of operators, quantises the way its compiler decides, and the compiler may not be yours to download — some are never distributed outside their home market. The model that trained overnight on a cluster meets a chip that cannot run half of it, and a driver that crashes on the first layer it does not know.
edge_ai.scar_p2: The datasheet says TOPS. It does not say which parts of your model will quietly run on the CPU instead, or that the stock driver delivers a quarter of the speed the silicon has. Those answers come from running models on the chip, and we have been doing that since the first camera SoCs with a vision engine — starting on ARM cores with no floating-point unit at all.
edge_ai.scar_title: Your model does not run here, and nobody will tell you why
edge_ai.stat_fps_l: licence plates read on a camera chip, end to end
edge_ai.stat_gap_l: the speed a stock driver leaves on the table, measured on the same chip
edge_ai.stat_loss_l: of the model's accuracy kept after fitting it to the chip
edge_ai.stats_source: Measured by us on RK3588 and HiSilicon silicon, on models we fitted and drivers we wrote.
edge_ai.step1_text: Fixed price, five working days. You send the model or its architecture, the SoC and SDK version, about fifty frames from the real camera, and the numbers you are judged on. You get a layer-by-layer verdict on what runs, the accuracy at stake in fitting it to the chip and how to keep it, the speed to expect against our measured baselines, and a fixed quote for the next step.
edge_ai.step2_text: The model reshaped and retrained on your footage, running entirely on the accelerator in a lean native runtime, measured on your board. Acceptance is the numbers agreed in the report.
edge_ai.step3_text: Into OpenIPC or your firmware, CI under QEMU where the chip is covered, driver work where the stack is missing — and a retainer for the SDK churn that locks models to firmware versions.
edge_ai.title: Edge AI

get_started.editions_text: Lite fits 8 MB flash chips and covers the essentials. Ultimate adds extras like cloud streaming, tunnels, and more codecs — it needs 16 MB flash.
get_started.hero_lede: From stock firmware to OpenIPC in about half an hour — with a guide generated for your exact chip.
get_started.hero_title: Give your camera a second life.
get_started.step1_text_html: Run ipctool on the camera (telnet or serial console) to learn the SoC, the sensor, and the flash chip. A label or FCC ID search works as a fallback.
get_started.step2_text: Look your chip up in the supported hardware table. The wizard assembles a firmware image and a step-by-step installation guide for your exact configuration, right in your browser.
get_started.step3_text: Follow the generated guide. It starts with a full backup of the stock firmware — do not skip it.
get_started.stuck_text_html: The community answers questions every day. Ask in the chat — include your SoC, sensor, and a boot log if you have one.
get_started.title: Get Started
get_started.wall_text_html: One setting in the web interface puts your camera's snapshots on our live Open Wall — say hello to the community.
get_started.warning_text_html: Flashing can brick a camera. The guide shows you how to make a full backup first, and Coupler can handle the safe path on supported models. If in doubt, ask in the chat before you flash.
get_started.what_text: A clean Linux system with the Majestic streamer: RTSP, ONVIF, WebRTC, and HLS out of the box, a web interface, and full root access. Your camera, actually yours.

green_life.paragraph1: OpenIPC contributes to sustainability by primarily providing open firmware for IP cameras, directly engaging in the efficient use and repurposing of existing hardware.
green_life.paragraph2: By extending the lifespan of cameras through customizable firmware updates and features, OpenIPC reduces electronic waste.
green_life.paragraph3: This aligns with sustainability goals by promoting the reuse and repurposing of technology, minimizing the environmental impact associated with the production and disposal of electronic devices.
green_life.paragraph4: Additionally, OpenIPC's commitment to transparency and community-driven development fosters a collaborative approach to technology, encouraging users to actively engage and contribute to the project's growth and sustainability.
green_life.title: Green Life

isp_sensors.bring1_text: Sixty frames, binning, cropped high-speed windows. We derive the timings from the datasheet and verify them on the interface, so the mode you need exists on your board.
isp_sensors.bring1_title: Modes the vendor did not ship
isp_sensors.bring2_text: When a port runs slow, the cause is in the init sequence or the pipeline, not the sensor. We trace the vendor firmware register by register and rebuild the path until the rate matches the silicon.
isp_sensors.bring3_text: We know which statistics are measured where — before or after dehaze, on raw or on colour — so your loops close on data they can act on. Delivered as a report with before-and-after captures.
isp_sensors.bring4_text: A genealogy of which sensors are rebrands of which, and a porting guide that collapses eight platform generations into five driver tiers, so the second port costs a fraction of the first.
isp_sensors.brings_intro: Four things, each one measured on the hardware.
isp_sensors.cta_note_html: Commercial support, OEM licensing and the other services are on the business page.
isp_sensors.cta_text: One mail with four lines: the sensor and SoC, the mode or picture you need, what you have today, and your volume and timeline. An engineer answers with a plan, not a sales script.
isp_sensors.cta_title: Send the sensor and the board. In ten days you will know what frame rate it can really do.
isp_sensors.eyebrow: Whitepaper · ISP & sensors · Drivers, modes and image quality
isp_sensors.hero_cta_send: Send us the sensor and the board
isp_sensors.hero_lede: A camera is a sensor, an image pipeline and a driver that must agree with both. We port sensors to new silicon, recover the modes the vendor driver never exposed, and tune the pipeline so the picture is measured rather than guessed.
isp_sensors.hero_title: The sensor your datasheet promised, at the frame rate it promised.
isp_sensors.meta_description: Sensor driver porting and image-pipeline tuning on HiSilicon, SigmaStar, Ingenic and Rockchip camera SoCs: the modes the datasheet promised, at the frame rate it promised, measured rather than guessed.
isp_sensors.platforms_text: More than 160 sensor drivers across ten chip families, and firmware shipping on hundreds of sensor-and-SoC pairings. If your combination exists, we have probably booted it; if it does not, we know what the port costs before we start.
isp_sensors.pull_quote: Exposure there is a ceiling, not a time. Once you know that, the tuning makes sense.
isp_sensors.res1_text: A 5-megapixel sensor with wide dynamic range ran at a broken 6 fps on a customer-grade camera. Tracing the vendor's init sequence and rewriting the pipeline took it to 21 — a few frames short of the vendor's own closed build, with the dynamic range kept on. The recordings are the proof.
isp_sensors.res2_text: Porting a 1080p60 mode from datasheet timings cut sensor-side latency by a full frame and lifted the encoded rate on the wire by 47%. The same method gave a 4K sensor runtime crop and binning up to 200 fps. Every mode was verified on the interface, not in a log.
isp_sensors.res3_text: A fog tuning of two cameras doubled the measurable detail on one and cut its haze by four fifths — with every cost itemised, and two vendor knobs shown to do nothing. It came with a finding the documentation omits: exposure statistics are taken upstream of dehaze, so a software tone loop cannot close on them.
isp_sensors.scar_p1: You chose the sensor for what the datasheet promised — wide dynamic range, sixty frames, a 4K window — and got a driver that runs one mode at one rate, with a register table copied from a reference board. Changing anything means a vendor ticket, and the vendor's answer is the mode you already have.
isp_sensors.scar_p2: Tuning is worse. The pipeline reports statistics from a stage you cannot see, so the exposure loop you wrote never converges and nobody can tell you why. You need people who have read the pipeline's actual data flow — across eight generations of one vendor's silicon, and four vendors.
isp_sensors.scar_title: The datasheet has six modes. Your driver has one.
isp_sensors.stat1_l: up from a broken 6 on the same silicon — a 5-megapixel sensor with wide dynamic range kept on
isp_sensors.stat2_l: of sensor-side latency removed by one ported mode
isp_sensors.stat3_l: from a 4K sensor in a cropped window, with crop and binning set at runtime
isp_sensors.stats_source: Measured by us on shipping camera hardware; the before-and-after recordings are shown on the call.
isp_sensors.step1_text: Fixed price, ten working days. You send the sensor and SoC — or a sample unit — your current driver or firmware, and the mode or picture you need. You get the measured frame rate and latency of what you have, the modes the silicon can reach, the cause of any gap, and a port plan with a fixed quote.
isp_sensors.step2_text: Port or rewrite the driver, verify the timings on the interface, tune against before-and-after captures, and hand over the register tables with the reasoning behind every value.
isp_sensors.step3_text: Drivers land in your tree, or in OpenIPC if you prefer shared maintenance, with genealogy notes for the next sensor you choose.
isp_sensors.title: ISP and sensors

low_latency.build_apfpv_text: Plain WiFi instead of broadcast. The air unit runs an access point and the ground station joins it, so anything with a WiFi adapter can receive the stream.
low_latency.build_fpv_text: The OpenIPC link, and what the build guide sets up. wfb-ng broadcasts the video with no pairing and no association, and adaptive-link moves the bitrate as the signal changes.
low_latency.build_rubyfpv_text: For a RubyFPV ground station. RubyFPV's own link and telemetry take the place of wfb-ng; the camera side is otherwise the same.
low_latency.builds_lede: Three builds of the air unit, differing in the radio link and nothing else. Which one you want is decided by what is at the other end.
low_latency.builds_title: Pick the build to match your ground station
low_latency.business_bridge_html: Building a product on this link? Talk to us — we do custom development and OEM work.
low_latency.credits_text_html: The radio link exists thanks to wfb-ng and devourer, and the ecosystem grows with friends like RubyFPV and Mario FPV. Open source is a team sport.
low_latency.fpv_text: A fully open digital FPV system: no locked ecosystem, no paired hardware, no firmware ceiling. Build the air unit from a supported camera, pick your ground station, and tune every stage of the pipeline.
low_latency.hardware_text_html: Air units are built from supported cameras and AIO boards — start from the supported hardware list. RunCam and other vendors ship OpenIPC-based FPV hardware out of the box.
low_latency.hero_lede: FPV drones, robots, teleoperation: an open ultra-low-latency video stack from camera to screen. Glass-to-glass from about 30 ms on supported hardware.
low_latency.hero_title: Open video links for machines that can't wait.
low_latency.how_link_text_html: devourer carries video, telemetry, and control over commodity Realtek adapters, straight from userspace — no association, no retransmit stalls, and rate, power and channel set per frame.
low_latency.how_rx_text_html: PixelPilot turns a Rockchip board into a dedicated ground station — the fastest way to receive. Aviateur runs on the Windows, Linux, or macOS machine you already own.
low_latency.how_tx_text_html: An OpenIPC camera runs the Waybeam encoder, turning the sensor into a stream and handing it straight to the radio. The frame rate set here decides most of your latency budget.
low_latency.latency_intro: What decides your number is the ground station, far more than the resolution you pick. These are figures people report from flying this stack on their own hardware.
low_latency.latency_note: Reported in the OpenIPC and wfb-ng chats, not measured by us. Resolution barely moves the number; frame rate and screen refresh decide it — change nothing but the monitor and the same camera shifts by 120 ms.
low_latency.robotics_text1: The same link carries video for industrial robots, AGVs, inspection rigs, and remote operation — anywhere a closed video system would lock you in or a cloud hop would add seconds.
low_latency.robotics_text2: On supported SoCs, frames carry wall-clock timestamps tied to the sensor frame start — millisecond-class synchronization for multi-camera rigs without extra hardware.
low_latency.title: Low-Latency Video

majestic_endpoints.moved_html: The list of endpoints your camera serves now lives in the camera's own web interface, under Majestic → Endpoints. Open http://<camera-address>/ in a browser and pick it from the menu.
majestic_endpoints.reason_address: your camera's real address is filled in, so a URL can be copied straight into a player;
majestic_endpoints.reason_auth: it says whether the endpoints ask for a password, or whether authentication has been switched off entirely.
majestic_endpoints.reason_scheme: the scheme matches your setup, http or https and ws or wss;
majestic_endpoints.title: Majestic Endpoints
majestic_endpoints.why: It is generated there from the firmware that is actually running, which a page on this site cannot be:

our_team.paragraph1_html: OpenIPC is a community-driven open source project, and many people contribute to its codebase. Kudos to them! There is also a core team of skilled developers who work hard to expand the list of supported hardware platforms, extend the functionality and stability of the firmware, review submitted code, and coordinate community efforts. Get to know the team and their areas of expertise:
our_team.title: Our Team

privacy.contact_note_html: There is no account to delete and no profile to export, because we do not build one — but if something here is unclear or looks wrong, we would rather hear it.
privacy.contact_title: Ask us about any of this
privacy.counting_lede: A counter we run ourselves, on the same server that serves the site. Nothing goes to anyone else.
privacy.hero_lede: We measure openipc.org so we can tell whether its pages do their job. This page says exactly what that means. It is short because a long one is a promise nobody checks.
privacy.log_lede: The ordinary record every web server keeps.
privacy.log_text_html: Each request is written to a log with the address it came from, the page, and the result. We use it to find faults, to stop abuse, and to size the machine. It is deleted after 14 days.
privacy.never_cookies_html: No cookie, no local storage, no identifier of any kind. Nothing is kept in your browser.
privacy.never_individuals_html: No individual visits. Only daily totals reach the disk, so there is no row anywhere that is you.
privacy.never_region_html: No region or city. That needs a finer location database than we keep.
privacy.records_clicks_html: Clicks that leave the site: writing to us, joining the chat, opening a donation page, or following a link elsewhere.
privacy.records_device_html: Your browser and operating system, and the size of your screen.
privacy.records_page_html: The page you opened, and the site you came from if your browser sent one.
privacy.records_place_html: Your country, and the language your browser asks for.
privacy.records_tag_html: A tag in the address, such as ?ref=tg-ru, when we posted the link ourselves. It is counted once and then removed from the address.
privacy.sessions_html: To count one person reading three pages as one visit rather than three, the counter derives a short-lived key from your address and browser. It exists in memory for at most eight hours and is never written down. Your address is not stored by the counter at all.
privacy.sessions_title: The one thing that sounds like tracking
privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.wall_lede: Cameras running OpenIPC can send a picture to the wall. This part is about the camera, not about you.
privacy.wall_published_html: Published: the picture, and what the camera says about itself — chip, sensor, firmware, streamer, uptime and chip temperature.
privacy.wall_retention_html: A nightly sweep removes pictures, and the descriptions that came with them, once they are 2 days old, so nothing stays beyond 3.
privacy.wall_withheld_html: Not published: the camera's MAC and IP addresses, both visible only to maintainers. The MAC decides two things: one camera may upload every 15 minutes, and a camera on the block list is refused. Each camera's page is named by a token that cannot be turned back into either address.

reverse_engineering.bring1_text: Kernel drivers and firmware you can build, patch and carry to the next kernel. We replace the binary function by function and prove parity by comparing traces.
reverse_engineering.bring2_text: Each deliverable ships with its oracle: a register-parity check, an on-air witness with a positive control, a byte-identical output. If a claim cannot be tested, we say so.
reverse_engineering.bring3_text: Binary model formats, encrypted SDKs, modified weights. We recover layouts down to the register map and modifications down to the exact layers changed — and hand the running of them to our Edge AI team.
reverse_engineering.bring4_text: AI-assisted decompilation and an in-house decompiler with type recovery let one engineer cover what used to take a team. The hardware still has the last word.
reverse_engineering.bring4_title: Faster than it used to be
reverse_engineering.brings_intro: Four things, each one measured on the hardware.
reverse_engineering.cta_note_html: Commercial support, OEM licensing and the other services are on the business page.
reverse_engineering.cta_text: One mail with four lines: what the target is, what you need from it, what you can share, and the deadline. Under NDA from the first reply. An engineer answers, not a sales script.
reverse_engineering.cta_title: Send the binary and the question. In five days you will know whether the answer can be proven.
reverse_engineering.eyebrow: Whitepaper · Reverse engineering · Hardware, software and neural networks
reverse_engineering.hero_cta_send: Send us the binary and the question
reverse_engineering.hero_lede: When the documentation is missing, the vendor is gone, or the blob is the product, we recover what the silicon actually does — from disassembly, from traces, from the air — and prove it with a harness that answers yes or no. We have used IDA since the 1990s; the automation is newer, the discipline is not.
reverse_engineering.hero_title: Every claim verified on hardware. That is the whole method.
reverse_engineering.meta_description: Reverse engineering of hardware, firmware, protocols and neural networks, with custom harnesses that prove every recovered fact on the target hardware. Using IDA since the 1990s; AI-assisted where it helps.
reverse_engineering.platforms_text: Harnesses we build to prove the work: chip models that run vendor code on the desktop, kernel probes, USB monitors, register-parity oracles, on-air witnesses with positive controls, and conformance suites for the protocols your product speaks.
reverse_engineering.pull_quote: A decompiler tells you what the code might do. The harness tells you what it did.
reverse_engineering.res1_text: Two video-encoder kernel blobs became C, all 427 functions, verified by trace comparison on a desktop model of the chip. Cleanroom drivers for the same vendor's vision and neural engines came out byte-identical to the originals, and the firmware builds them on a current kernel.
reverse_engineering.res2_text: A mainstream Wi-Fi chipset's firmware protocol was specified from vendor sources, validated on air, and now drives 18 adapter types from userspace. A camera vendor's undocumented upgrade protocol — and the account hidden inside it — became a written specification. A motorised-lens protocol was reversed the same way, for autofocus.
reverse_engineering.res3_text: A camera NPU's binary model format was dissected to its register map. An encrypted commercial licence-plate SDK gave up its model layout from a running container. A modified language model was compared weight by weight and the modification recovered exactly, to the layer.
reverse_engineering.scar_p1: A kernel blob that pins you to an old kernel. A radio firmware with an interface nobody documented. A model file the vendor will not explain. A device whose upgrade path you have to trust. The vendor's answer is a newer blob, or no answer at all.
reverse_engineering.scar_p2: Reverse engineering with a tool that guesses is worse than none. We have watched a language model write a fluent, wrong story about a binary. So every recovered fact is checked against running hardware — registers compared, packets witnessed on air, outputs matched byte for byte — before it enters the report.
reverse_engineering.scar_title: You depend on something you cannot read
reverse_engineering.stat1_l: encoder kernel functions replaced by readable C, validated by trace comparison against the original
reverse_engineering.stat2_l: Wi-Fi adapter types driven from userspace after one chipset's firmware protocol was specified from sources and the air
reverse_engineering.stat3_l: lines of decompilation read to recover one vendor's upgrade protocol — and the undocumented account inside it
reverse_engineering.stats_source: Each result validated on the target hardware or a bit-exact model of it; the harnesses are shown on the call.
reverse_engineering.step1_text: Fixed price, five working days. You send the binary, firmware image or device, and the question you need answered. You get what is recoverable, the harness we would build to prove it, the risks, and a fixed quote for the recovery.
reverse_engineering.step2_text: Harness first, then the recovery against it — driver, protocol, format or model — with every claim traceable to a test that your team can rerun.
reverse_engineering.step3_text: Source, specification, harness and oracles are yours. After every change, the proof runs again.
reverse_engineering.title: Reverse engineering

stages_of_firmware_development.done_info: Done and done! Bootloader boots, Linux loads, streamer can stream video and produce snaphots. You can have yourself a working platform open for tinkering and further improvements. We still expect feedback and patches from you guys, though.
stages_of_firmware_development.hlp_info: Help wanted. We have the hardware, we have the SDK, the basic stuff is learned and done. But we are stuck. This is where we are looking for help from experienced embedded developers to overcome the obstacles and move on to the next stage.
stages_of_firmware_development.mvp_info: A minimal viable product. The basic system is built, the platform can produce video, at least on the main channel, but due to a lack of human resources, development is delayed or halted. A financial infusion could push the development to the final stage.
stages_of_firmware_development.neq_info_html: No Equipment. We have an SDK for the platform, but we don't have specific hardware to continue development, you can donate it to our R&D guys (especially old boards that passed <abbr title="End-Of-Life">EOL</abbr> and can not longer be bought).
stages_of_firmware_development.paragraph1: After we acquire an SDK for a new SoC, we add the SoC to the table of supported hardware. We assign either NEQ (No Equipment) status, if we do not have particular hardware modules, or HLP (Help Needed) status, if we have the hardware but are looking for a developer who would lead the development for that SoC. This is considered an official start of development.
stages_of_firmware_development.paragraph2: There is no reason to have SoC in the table without having its SDK.
stages_of_firmware_development.paragraph3: As work on the SoC progresses, its status changes, gradually. First to RND, then to WIP, then further to MVP, and, finally, to DONE.
stages_of_firmware_development.rnd_info: The Research and Development stage, when we already have the platform SDK and maybe even the hardware boards, but we are starting to fiddle with the platform, studying its specifics and features. There is still a lot of work ahead.
stages_of_firmware_development.subtitle: Typical development lifecycle
stages_of_firmware_development.title: Stages of Firmware development
stages_of_firmware_development.wip_info: Work in progress. We learned a lot about the platform hardware and code base, prepared the first public binary build, and are waiting for the first adopters to test it on their boards and provide feedback to help us move forward.

teleoperation.bring_latency_text: The same stack FPV pilots fly at full speed, on cameras that cost less than lunch. Open firmware from the sensor to the encoder, tuned for the shortest way out.
teleoperation.bring_latency_title: Tens of milliseconds, proven in the air
teleoperation.bring_link_text: Video down, control up, and no stall in between: no pairing, no retransmit queue. When the air gets noisy you lose a frame, never the robot.
teleoperation.bring_link_title: A link that drops a frame, not the operator
teleoperation.bring_stream_text: One encoded stream, two speeds. The recorder keeps every frame while the operator's link carries what it can — no second encoder, no second camera.
teleoperation.bring_time_text: Each frame is stamped the instant the sensor captures it, before anything else touches it. Every camera on the robot agrees to within a few milliseconds, with no trigger cable, so the dataset lines up.
teleoperation.brings_intro: Four things, each already running on cameras in the field.
teleoperation.brings_title: What OpenIPC brings to the loop
teleoperation.cta_note_html: An engineer answers, not a sales script. Camera and link engineering that ships today is on the business page.
teleoperation.cta_text: We are taking three design partners: a robot, a bench and an engineer on your side; camera firmware, the link and our time on ours. What comes out is a teleoperation loop measured on your machine — and, if you want it, your first dataset.
teleoperation.cta_title: Bring a robot, whoever made it. We bring the eyes.
teleoperation.hero_art_alt: An operator in a VR headset mirrored by a humanoid robot working in a flooded industrial plant
teleoperation.hero_cta_pilot: Talk to us about a pilot
teleoperation.hero_lede: OpenIPC brings the open, ultra-low-latency video stack proven in FPV to human-in-the-loop robotics: a rig that fits any robot from any maker, a link that never stalls, every frame stamped the instant it is captured, every session a dataset.
teleoperation.hero_title: A hundred humanoids are about to learn from people. Give them eyes that keep up.
teleoperation.landscape_p1: Everyone building a general-purpose robot has picked a way to get training data. Figure bets on human video, Tesla on simulation, 1X and Unitree on human-in-the-loop teleoperation: a person drives the robot, the session is recorded, and a policy is trained on data that is already kinematically correct for that body. Amazon's research teams take the other road, translating human motion capture into robot motion after the fact.
teleoperation.landscape_p2: Teleoperation is winning because it closes the embodiment gap at the source. Unitree alone has built some 18,000 bipeds, and every one of them is going to be driven.
teleoperation.landscape_p3: What is not settled is the rig. Unitree's avatar drives Unitree's robot. The other 43 makers on the list, and every lab with more than one kind of machine, need a teleoperation and data rig that fits any robot and any camera.
teleoperation.landscape_p4: And it has to answer the one question demo videos never do: what is the glass-to-glass figure, and how was it measured? The operator can only be as good as the delay they feel, and the dataset inherits every hesitation.
teleoperation.landscape_title: The data strategy is settled. The rig is not.
teleoperation.loop_intro: Teleoperator is the layer we are building on top of the stack: a human-in-the-loop rig for any robot — humanoid, wheeled or flying — piloted from a headset, with every session written as LeRobot datasets the open robotics community already trains on.
teleoperation.loop_return: The policy trained on the dataset drives the robot next. That is the flywheel.
teleoperation.loop_title: From the operator's hands to the training set
teleoperation.meta_description: Open ultra-low-latency video for robot teleoperation: a rig that fits any robot, a link that never stalls, every frame stamped at capture, every session a dataset.
teleoperation.node_operator_text: Sees what the robot sees; head, hands or whole body tracked
teleoperation.node_recorder_text: Every frame, every pose, one clock
teleoperation.node_robot_text: Any maker's: arms, legs, wheels or rotors
teleoperation.pilot1_text: OpenIPC firmware on the cameras your robot already carries, and the link between the robot and the operator's station.
teleoperation.pilot2_text: An operator drives the machine: head and hands from a headset, or the whole body from a motion-capture suit, mapped onto the robot's own joints, with a failsafe that stops it the moment the link goes quiet.
teleoperation.pilot3_text: Folding laundry, loading a fridge, tidying a room: every run is recorded on one clock — what the operator saw, what they did, what the robot felt — as LeRobot episodes, ready to train on.
teleoperation.pull_quote: Latency is a tax on every episode you record.
teleoperation.stat_latency_l: glass-to-glass on the OpenIPC stack, camera to screen
teleoperation.stat_units_l: units expected to ship in 2026, most of them to labs
teleoperation.stats_source_html: Market figures: KeyResearch, September 2026. Latency: figures reported by people flying the stack, on the low-latency page.
teleoperation.title: Teleoperation
teleoperation.why1_text: Firmware and tools for dozens of camera chip families, in the open, with a community that reads the source and fixes what it finds.
teleoperation.why2_text: FPV pilots fly the stack every day, and RunCam and other vendors ship OpenIPC-based hardware out of the box. The reflexes that fly a drone through a gap are the ones that box a robot in a ring, and the link has already been through the worst radio conditions there are.
teleoperation.why3_text: No cloud, no subscription, no per-unit tax, and no dependency on whose robot you bought. When a chip goes end-of-life, the firmware outlives it — and so does your robot.
teleoperation.why3_title: Not tied to a robot maker

turnkey_hardware.bring1_text: Sensor, SoC, radio and power chosen against the software they must run, not the other way round. The firmware engineer sits in the schematic review.
turnkey_hardware.bring2_text: Boards boot an image that already runs on dozens of chip families, with the recovery, update and provisioning paths your fleet will need from the first unit.
turnkey_hardware.bring3_text: A blind recovery channel over the card slot and a serviceable update path mean a field unit is never a brick and the factory never needs a debugger.
turnkey_hardware.bring4_text: Power, thermal and frame-rate budgets are measured on the board. One sequencing change was worth 4.5 °C; you only find that with the board and the firmware on the same bench.
turnkey_hardware.brings_intro: Four things, each one measured on the hardware.
turnkey_hardware.cta_note_html: Commercial support, OEM licensing and the other services are on the business page.
turnkey_hardware.cta_text: One mail with four lines: what the product does, the sensor and link requirements, the power, enclosure and cost target, and your volume and timeline. An engineer answers with a plan, not a sales script.
turnkey_hardware.cta_title: Send the product brief. In ten days you will have a board the firmware team already agrees with.
turnkey_hardware.eyebrow: Whitepaper · Turnkey hardware · Board and firmware from one team
turnkey_hardware.hero_lede: Fitting software into someone else's board is how products ship late with a feature crossed out. We design the board and the firmware as one product — sensor, SoC, power, radio, enclosure, and the software that has to live in it.
turnkey_hardware.hero_title: One team draws the board and writes the firmware — so neither apologises for the other.
turnkey_hardware.meta_description: Board and firmware designed by one team: sensor, SoC, power, radio and the software that has to live in it, delivered as a balanced product instead of software squeezed into someone else's hardware.
turnkey_hardware.platforms_text: Camera and edge boards around the SoCs the firmware already runs on, sensors from the catalogue we maintain, analogue, IP and radio-linked video, in small and medium volumes. Design files and firmware source are deliverables, not licences.
turnkey_hardware.pull_quote: The bug was a wire. It was found by the person who needed the wire.
turnkey_hardware.res1_text: Our reference boards are 38 × 38 mm analogue-video cameras on a low-cost SoC, in three variants, with the pinout at revision 1.4 this September. They exist because board and firmware were drawn together, and they are the pattern for your product.
turnkey_hardware.res2_text: USB device bring-up on a camera SoC uncovered a hardware gap — a missing sense line — that no firmware could bridge. In review it is a wire; in the field it is a spin. Co-design puts the finding in the review.
turnkey_hardware.res3_text: The firmware runs on dozens of SoC families and hundreds of sensor pairings, with recovery over serial and card slot for more than 120 chips. Your product inherits the streaming, recovery and update stack and the team that maintains it. What is specific to you stays yours.
turnkey_hardware.scar_p1: You have a product idea and two quotes: a hardware house that will build any board you specify, and a firmware team that will make any board work. Each is right, and the gap between them is where the schedule goes — the sense line nobody routed, the sensor that cannot reach its frame rate on that SoC, the thermal budget the enclosure ate.
turnkey_hardware.scar_p2: We have been the firmware team on that call. One camera bring-up stopped on a single missing sense wire: the USB port could never know it was plugged in, and no software could cover for it. Found late, that is a board spin. Found in schematic review by the engineer who needs the wire, it costs nothing.
turnkey_hardware.scar_title: Two quotes, and the schedule falls in the gap between them
turnkey_hardware.stat1_l: our reference camera board line, pinout published at revision 1.4
turnkey_hardware.stat2_l: of SoC families the firmware already boots on, so a new board runs a working image on day one
turnkey_hardware.stat3_l: cooler from one power-sequencing change, measured on the board rather than read from a datasheet
turnkey_hardware.stats_source: Our reference camera line, designed by our hardware engineer and shipping under a partner brand; measurements taken on our own boards.
turnkey_hardware.step1_text: Fixed price, ten working days. You send what the product must do: optics, resolution and frame rate, interfaces, link, enclosure, power source, cost target, volume. You get a block diagram, a sensor-and-SoC shortlist with measured frame-rate and power budgets, a bill-of-materials estimate, the risks, and a schedule with a fixed quote for the first prototype run.
turnkey_hardware.step2_text: Schematic, layout and firmware in one team; prototypes measured on the bench; a pilot run with provisioning and recovery in place before the first unit ships.
turnkey_hardware.step3_text: Design files, firmware source and test fixtures are yours, with optional shared maintenance in OpenIPC for the parts that are not specific to you.
turnkey_hardware.title: Turnkey hardware

utilities.paragraph1: A collection of useful tools and utilities.
utilities.title: Utilities

video_encoding.bring1_text: Savings compound over the life of a stream: fewer bytes on every second of every camera, every month, from settings the default path never exposes.
video_encoding.bring2_text: We score with a composite of three perceptual metrics, not one number that can be gamed. When a configuration wins, it wins on all three, or we tell you why not.
video_encoding.bring3_text: No new hardware, no licence. The gains come from rate control, lookahead, quantisation maps and mode choices that sit unused in the encoder you have.
video_encoding.bring4_text: We tune the encoder on a five-dollar camera chip with the same rigour as a data-centre GPU, including layered streams that let one encode serve live view and recording.
video_encoding.brings_intro: Four things, each one measured on the hardware.
video_encoding.cta_note_html: Commercial support, OEM licensing and the other services are on the business page.
video_encoding.cta_text: One mail with four lines: the encoder platform and codec, the content and resolution, what you want to cut, and where the clips can be picked up. An engineer answers with a plan, not a sales script.
video_encoding.cta_title: Send three clips. In ten days you will know what your encoder is leaving on the table.
video_encoding.eyebrow: Whitepaper · Video encoding · Hardware encoders and modern codecs
video_encoding.hero_lede: Your encoder is already paid for, and most of it is never switched on. We tune hardware encoders on NVIDIA, Intel, Rockchip and HiSilicon silicon — and the camera chips upstream of them — so you ship the same quality at lower bitrate, measured on your own content rather than a vendor's demo clip.
video_encoding.hero_title: The same encoder, fewer bits — and a better picture.
video_encoding.meta_description: Hardware video-encoder evaluation and tuning on NVIDIA, Intel, Rockchip and HiSilicon silicon, and on camera chips: the same quality at lower bitrate, measured on your own content.
video_encoding.platforms_text: Hardware encoders on desktop, server and embedded silicon; software encoders where they still win; the camera-side encoders in OpenIPC firmware. Scored with perceptual metrics validated against the reference implementation, on your content.
video_encoding.pull_quote: Tune the baseline before you claim to beat it.
video_encoding.res1_text: A 5 W embedded encoder beat a desktop GPU by 8–13% bitrate at 4K in HEVC, at an order of magnitude lower cost. Its H.264 was weaker, and we say so — the right choice depends on the decoders you must serve. The whole study is published, presets and all.
video_encoding.res2_text: NVIDIA and Intel encoders measured across low-latency and quality presets in H.264, HEVC and AV1, against the software encoders they are sold to replace, in a comparison database we keep current. Every result comes with its method, so your team can rerun it on your content.
video_encoding.res3_text: On the camera chips we ship firmware for, the encoder's reference structure alone makes a static scene 3.1× cheaper to stream, and a lost packet costs one frame instead of a whole group. We know each chip's real pixel-rate ceiling and put temporal layers on two platforms so one stream serves three consumers.
video_encoding.scar_p1: A hardware encoder is chosen for frames per second, and the driver's defaults were written for a demo, not for your content. Every percent of bitrate you do not reclaim is paid monthly — in egress, in storage, in the radio link that drops a frame under load — for as long as the product lives.
video_encoding.scar_p2: Vendor numbers will not help you, because each was measured against a badly configured competitor. We have watched most of an apparent win evaporate once the baseline was set up properly. You need someone who tunes your baseline first, and only then tells you what is left on the table.
video_encoding.scar_title: You bought throughput and accepted the quality it came with
video_encoding.stat1_l: fewer bits than a desktop GPU at 4K, from an embedded encoder that draws 5 W
video_encoding.stat2_l: cheaper static-scene streams from the encoder's reference structure alone
video_encoding.stat3_l: to bit-exact recovery after a lost packet, with the structure we ship
video_encoding.stats_source: Measured by us on stock hardware and on camera chips we ship firmware for; our engineers publish the encoder work on vmetrix.tech.
video_encoding.step1_text: Fixed price, ten working days. You send three representative clips, your encoder platform and settings, and the target — bitrate, storage or quality. You get your baseline tuned and measured, a recommended configuration, and the saving at equal quality on your own content, with the scores behind it.
video_encoding.step2_text: We implement it in your pipeline: the API path, rate control, quantisation maps, temporal layers — validated on your fleet's content mix, on the hardware you run.
video_encoding.step3_text: You own the settings, the measurement harness and the report. Rerun it when the content or the hardware changes; call us when the answer surprises you.
video_encoding.title: Video encoding
